item.title: Anatomy of an Investment Policy Statement
item.summary: An investment policy statement (IPS) is a written plan for a portfolio, built from a set of standard parts. Knowing what each part does lets you place any IPS clause in the right section, which is a common exam task.

sections.heading: The IPS as a blueprint
sections.body_markdown:
Think of building a house. Before anyone lays a brick, you need a blueprint that says who the house is for, what it must do, what limits apply (budget, zoning), what materials are allowed, and who inspects the work. An **investment policy statement (IPS)** is that blueprint for a portfolio. It is a written document, tailored to one client, that guides how the portfolio is planned, run and checked.

Because every client differs, the standard list of sections is a checklist, not a form to fill in. Not every section matters equally for every client, and extra sections can be added for unusual circumstances.

sections.heading: The first half: who, why and how it is run
sections.body_markdown:
A common Level I breakdown of an IPS has these parts. The first four set the scene and the rules of the game:

1. **Client description (introduction):** who the client is, such as an individual, family, pension plan or foundation, and the relevant background (age, wealth, source of funds, nature of the institution).
2. **Statement of purpose:** why the document exists and what it is meant to achieve for this client.
3. **Duties and responsibilities:** who does what. The client, the investment adviser or manager, the custodian (the firm that holds the assets) and any trustee or committee each have assigned tasks, which creates accountability.
4. **Procedures:** how the IPS is kept up to date and what happens in particular situations, for example review at set intervals or when the client's circumstances change materially.

The contents pages of CFA Institute's IPS guides for individuals and institutions group similar items under headings such as scope and purpose and governance, so the labels vary between sources. The ideas are the same.

sections.heading: The middle: objectives, constraints and guidelines
sections.body_markdown:
These three parts say what the portfolio must achieve and what limits it.

- **Investment objectives:** what the portfolio is trying to achieve, expressed as a **return objective** (how much it needs or wants to earn) and a **risk objective** (how much risk it can and will take). Later lessons cover how to build these.
- **Investment constraints:** limits that restrict how the portfolio can be invested. The standard five are liquidity needs (cash needed for spending), time horizon, taxes, legal and regulatory factors, and unique circumstances or preferences. These come from the client's situation.
- **Investment guidelines:** practical rules for managing the portfolio. They cover what may be held or is prohibited, limits on concentration, whether leverage (borrowing to invest) or derivatives may be used, and similar items. These are the working rules for the manager. Constraints describe the client's situation, while guidelines are the manager's rulebook.

A simple memory aid: objectives are what you want, constraints are what limits you, and guidelines are the rules you will follow.

sections.heading: The last part: checking the work and the appendices
sections.body_markdown:
- **Evaluation and review:** how results are judged. This includes the **benchmark** (a reference portfolio or index used to judge performance), how often performance is reported and reviewed, and how the review is conducted.
- **Appendices:** supporting detail that is likely to change more often than the main text. Two typical appendices are the **strategic asset allocation** (the long-run target mix across asset classes, often with allowed ranges) and the **rebalancing policy** (how and when the portfolio is brought back to the targets).

IPS guidance says that outside boundaries for acceptable drift from targets should be documented. If the policy is not to rebalance, that should also be written down. Keeping these in an appendix lets the targets be updated without rewriting the whole IPS.

worked_example.problem: A wealth manager is drafting an IPS for a client. Match each clause to the IPS component it belongs in: (a) 'The custodian will hold all assets and send statements monthly.' (b) 'No more than 5% of the portfolio may be held in any one issuer.' (c) 'Performance will be compared with a blended equity and bond index and reported quarterly.' (d) 'The target mix is 60% equities and 40% bonds, with allowed ranges of ±5 percentage points.'
steps: Clause (a) assigns a task to a named party. That is a statement of duties and responsibilities.
Clause (b) is a rule on what the manager may hold and how concentrated the portfolio may be. That is an investment guideline.
Clause (c) names a benchmark and a reporting frequency. That belongs in evaluation and review.
Clause (d) gives a target mix and allowed ranges. That is the strategic asset allocation, usually placed in an appendix.

Check: none of these clauses describes the client's identity (client description), the reason for the IPS (purpose), the update process (procedures), the return or risk goals (objectives), or a limit such as liquidity or taxes (constraints).
worked_example.answer: (a) Duties and responsibilities; (b) investment guidelines; (c) evaluation and review; (d) strategic asset allocation appendix.

exam_traps: Mixing up constraints and guidelines. Constraints (liquidity, time horizon, taxes, legal, unique circumstances) come from the client's situation. Guidelines are rules on permitted holdings, leverage, derivatives and limits.
Treating the return objective as a constraint. Objectives say what the portfolio aims to achieve, while constraints limit how it can get there.

Putting benchmarks and reporting under procedures. Benchmarks, reporting frequency and the review process belong to evaluation and review. Procedures concern updating the IPS and handling specific situations.
Assuming every IPS must contain identical headings. Different sources group and name the parts differently, and not every element suits every investor, so focus on what each part does.
Forgetting the appendices. The strategic asset allocation and the rebalancing policy usually sit there, not in the main objectives section.

item.stem: An IPS states that the investment manager selects securities, the custodian holds the assets, and the investment committee approves any change to the policy. Which IPS component is this?

options.explanation: Objectives state return and risk goals. They do not assign tasks to parties.
This part covers benchmarks and how performance is reported and reviewed. It is not about who performs which task.
Correct. This component assigns tasks to named parties such as the client, manager, custodian and committee, which creates accountability.

item.stem: Which of the following statements would most appropriately appear as an investment guideline in an IPS?

options.text: The client will need $40,000 a year from the portfolio starting in three years.
options.explanation: This describes a cash need, which is a liquidity constraint from the client's situation. It is not a rule for the manager.

options.text: No single issuer may exceed 5% of the portfolio, and short selling is prohibited.
options.explanation: Correct. Limits on concentration and prohibited techniques are working rules for managing the portfolio, which is what guidelines are.

options.text: Results will be compared with a 60/40 equity and bond index each quarter.
options.explanation: Choosing a benchmark and a reporting interval is evaluation and review, not a guideline.

item.stem: An IPS says that performance will be measured against a specified benchmark and reported to the client every quarter. This clause belongs in which component?

options.explanation: Correct. Benchmarks, reporting frequency and the way performance is reviewed make up this component.
Constraints are limits from the client's situation, such as liquidity or taxes. A reporting schedule is not one.
The purpose explains why the document exists. It does not set out reporting mechanics.

item.stem: Which pair of items is most likely to be placed in appendices to the IPS?

options.text: The client's tax situation and legal restrictions
options.explanation: These are investment constraints, which belong in the main body of the IPS.

options.text: The return objective and the risk objective
options.explanation: Objectives are a core part of the main IPS, not supporting detail.

options.text: The strategic asset allocation and the rebalancing policy
options.explanation: Correct. The target mix with its ranges and the rules for rebalancing back to target are typical appendix items. They can be updated without rewriting the main text.

item.stem: An IPS says the document will be reviewed every year, and sooner if the client retires, inherits a large sum or has a major change in health. Which component does this describe?

options.explanation: That component assigns tasks to parties. It is not about when and how the IPS is updated.
Correct. Procedures cover how the IPS is kept current and what actions follow specific events or changes in circumstances.
Guidelines set rules on holdings and portfolio management. They are not rules for revising the document.

item.stem: Which statement best distinguishes investment objectives from investment constraints in an IPS?

options.text: Objectives state the return and risk the portfolio aims for, while constraints are limits such as liquidity, time horizon, taxes, legal factors and unique circumstances.
options.explanation: Correct. Objectives are what the portfolio is trying to achieve. Constraints are the client-specific limits on how it may be invested.

options.text: Objectives are limits such as liquidity and taxes, while constraints state the return and risk the portfolio aims for.
options.explanation: This reverses the two terms. Liquidity and taxes are constraints, and return and risk goals are objectives.

options.text: Objectives list the permitted and prohibited securities, while constraints list the benchmark and reporting dates.
options.explanation: Permitted and prohibited holdings are guidelines. Benchmarks and reporting dates belong to evaluation and review.

item.stem: An IPS opens by describing the client as a 52-year-old physician with a spouse, two children and wealth built mainly from a medical practice. Which component is this?

options.explanation: Background facts can feed constraints, but a general description of who the client is belongs in the introduction. It is not a limit on investing.
The purpose says why the IPS exists. It does not describe the client's personal background.
Correct. The introduction identifies the client and gives relevant background such as family, occupation and source of wealth.

item.front: List the major components of an IPS in the Level I framework.
item.back: Client description, statement of purpose, duties and responsibilities, procedures, investment objectives, investment constraints, investment guidelines, evaluation and review, and appendices (such as the strategic asset allocation and rebalancing policy).

item.front: Investment constraints vs investment guidelines: what is the difference?
item.back: Constraints are limits from the client's situation: liquidity, time horizon, taxes, legal and regulatory factors, and unique circumstances. Guidelines are working rules for managing the portfolio, such as permitted assets, concentration limits, and whether leverage or derivatives may be used.

item.front: What does the 'evaluation and review' component of an IPS contain?
item.back: The benchmark used to judge performance, how often performance is reported, and how the review is conducted.

item.front: What belongs in the appendices of an IPS?
item.back: Supporting detail that changes more often than the main text, typically the strategic asset allocation (targets and ranges) and the rebalancing policy.
